status: complete — 100 of 105 verses; the epistolary greeting (1:1-2) and closing (5:12-14) are unindexed; awaiting second-pass review
note: A letter to foreigners in the Dispersion, and the text the curriculum leans on for C17. Three entries carry prior citations from C14, C17, and C23, which serve as the calibration set. The household instructions in 2:18-3:7 are indexed for what they anchor, with the curriculum's own guard against loyalty that is used to keep someone in harm stated in the entries rather than left implicit.
prediction_note: The indexing order named 1 Peter 'the core text for C17, the Citizen-Stranger.' Five entries reach C17 (1:17-21, 2:11-12, 2:13-17, 3:13-17, 4:1-6) and two carry PR10. Whether that amounts to the core text or merely a strong one is left to the reviewer; the drafter wrote the prediction and should not grade it.
coverage_note: The greeting (1:1-2) and closing (5:12-14) are left out as in James. The greeting's address — 'foreigners in the Dispersion' — frames the whole letter and is picked up where the letter turns it into an instruction, at 1:17 and 2:11. No entry reaches PR24, PR27, or PR28, the three practices still unanchored anywhere in the index; 2:4-10 builds a house out of living stones, which shares an image with Virtue Construction and does none of what PR27 describes.

entries.pericope: Though now you don't see him, you rejoice
entries.connection: The letter opens on hope before it says a word about conduct, and the hope is set inside grief rather than after it: 'for a little while… you have been put to grief in various trials.' Joy is attributed to people who cannot see what they love. C19 begins with hope deliberately for the same reason, and C10 makes the same claim that joy is a consequence of where one stands, not of what one currently feels.

entries.pericope: The prophets searched; angels desire to look
entries.connection: The prophets are described as ministering a message whose time and subject they were still searching for — 'not to themselves, but to you.' This is the reading habit C06 teaches: the older text points past itself, and its first speakers did not hold the whole of what they carried. It shares subject matter with the Discipline of Unknowing but prescribes no posture to the reader, so PR04 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Prepare your minds for action; be sober
entries.connection: 'Be sober' is the verb from which the desert writers took nepsis, the name of the practice itself, and here it is joined to a specific object: 'not conforming yourselves according to your former lusts.' Readiness of mind against the old desires before they are acted on is Watchfulness in its source form. The holiness command that follows gives the reason for the attention, not a separate instruction.

entries.pericope: Pass the time of your living as foreigners here
entries.connection: The address of the letter — foreigners in the Dispersion — becomes an instruction: live out the stay as foreigners, in reverent fear. The ground given is a redemption 'not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers.' Residence without ultimate belonging (C17) and the loosening of what silver and gold can purchase (C18) are given one argument.

entries.pericope: All flesh is like grass; the word remains forever
entries.connection: Purification is measured by its outcome, 'sincere brotherly affection,' and the command is to love 'from the heart fervently' — the inner work proved by what it produces between people, which is the argument of C12. The Isaiah quotation sets that love against the transience of all human glory, which is the comparison C18 makes when it asks what is worth holding.

entries.pericope: As newborn babies, long for the pure milk
entries.connection: The list of things to put away — deceit, hypocrisy, envy, evil speaking — is the inventory of a soul in friction with others, the territory of C22. The image that follows is of an infant feeding 'that you may grow thereby': growth by nourishment rather than by effort, at the pace of a newborn. That is C25's picture, though the passage commands the longing rather than the patience, so PR14 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy
entries.connection: People rejected or of no account — 'no people' — are built as living stones into a house for God, the same stone the builders rejected becoming the cornerstone. C26's temple is built out of material that had no business carrying light. The closing line names the change as mercy received, and C19's door is the same: those who had not obtained mercy now have.

entries.pericope: Foreigners and pilgrims, by your good works which they see
entries.connection: C17 quotes these two verses in full as the pattern of the chapter. The mechanism is neither argument nor power but conduct observed by people who are speaking against the community — full participation in a society that suspects you, while the loyalty that shapes the conduct is held elsewhere. That is the Citizen-Stranger's definition stated as a command.

entries.pericope: As free, and not using your freedom for a cloak
entries.connection: Submission to human ordinance is grounded 'for the Lord's sake,' and immediately qualified: 'as free… as bondservants of God.' Obeying the laws gladly while the final loyalty rests above any decree is PR10's own wording of the practice. 'Honor all men' closes the paragraph, which is the practice's refusal of contempt stated without exception.

entries.pericope: When he was cursed, he didn't curse back
entries.connection: The instruction is addressed to household slaves with no legal exit from harsh masters, and the index does not lift it into counsel to remain under abuse; the same guard the curriculum attaches to PR26 applies here. What it anchors is the pattern in 2:21-23, offered as the example to follow: cursed, he did not curse back; suffering, he did not threaten, but handed judgment to God. That is Non-Retaliation in action and in speech, with its interior mechanism named. The closing image, sheep returned to the Shepherd, is the image C19 opens with.

entries.pericope: The hidden person of the heart
entries.connection: C23 cites 3:4 directly: value located in the hidden person of the heart, the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, precious in the sight of God. The surrounding verses describe a conduct that wins 'without a word' — the same mechanism as 2:12, made unwitnessed and unargued. The instruction to wives sits inside a first-century household code; the index anchors the location of value in the unseen, not the code's ordering of the household, and the PR26 guard applies here as well.

entries.pericope: Joint heirs of the grace of life
entries.connection: The husband is told to live with his wife 'according to knowledge,' giving honour, as a co-heir rather than a subordinate, and the reason given is that his prayers may otherwise be hindered. C14's claim is that the household is where formation is tested, and this verse makes domestic conduct a condition of the interior life rather than a separate department of it.

entries.pericope: Not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult, but blessing
entries.connection: The plainest statement of Non-Retaliation outside the Gospels, covering both action and speech, with blessing returned in place of the blow. Peter then quotes Psalm 34:12-16, the same psalm C15 takes as its witness, and from it the command to 'seek peace, and pursue it' — peace as something actively built toward, which is the Architecture of Peace aiming at repair rather than victory.

entries.pericope: Ready to give an answer, with humility and fear
entries.connection: The defence of hope is to be given to anyone who asks, but its manner is specified — humility, fear, a good conscience — so that those who slander are put to shame by the life rather than by the argument. C17's public-square posture. The practice tag is carried by 2:11-12 and 2:13-17, which state it more directly; repeating it here would add a count rather than an anchor.

entries.pericope: The righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God
entries.connection: The centre of the paragraph is the purpose clause — the righteous for the unrighteous, 'that he might bring you to God' — which is C19's door. Baptism is then defined against its outward reading: not the washing of the flesh but the answer of a good conscience toward God, the inward reading of an outward sign that C06 teaches. The preaching to the spirits in prison is among the most disputed verses in the New Testament and is left uninterpreted here.

entries.pericope: They think it is strange that you don't run with them
entries.connection: The cost of the citizen-stranger's posture is described from the other side: former companions find it strange and speak against it. The instruction to 'arm yourselves also with the same mind' and live the rest of one's time for the will of God rather than the desires of men is a resolve made in advance against a known pull, which is the forward attention of C20.

entries.pericope: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling
entries.connection: Hospitality is commanded with its characteristic failure named — grumbling — and gifts are to be used 'as good managers of the grace of God,' held for others rather than owned. C16's service and C14's household open door. Two tags were considered and declined. 'Love covers a multitude of sins' shares PR17's subject but describes what love does, not the act of shielding someone from exposure. Hospitality without grumbling shares PR20's subject, but nothing here breaks a routine for a guest; the grumbling is the host's, not a peevish guest's, so PR22 does not apply either.

entries.pericope: Don't be astonished at the fiery trial
entries.connection: C14 cites 4:19 directly, and the Scriptural Appendix names this passage as the ground of Unreciprocated Care: keep doing good while it hurts and entrust the soul to a faithful Creator. The drafter notes the attractor test without overriding the author: the passage is about being insulted for doing good, and PR22 is defined more narrowly as bearing with ungrateful behaviour from those one is helping. The overlap is real — doing good to people who answer it with insult — but the recipients of the good are not named as the ones insulting. The author's placement stands; a reviewer who disagrees is disagreeing with WMT A3.

entries.pericope: Not lording it over those entrusted to you
entries.connection: Three paired contrasts for those who hold authority — not under compulsion but willingly, not for gain but eagerly, not lording it but as examples — written by a man who calls himself a fellow elder rather than a superior. C16 opens by saying authority corrupts nearly everyone who holds it; this is the apostolic rule against each of the three corruptions.

entries.pericope: Clothe yourselves with humility; cast all your worries on him
entries.connection: Humility is commanded toward one another before it is commanded toward God, and it is pictured as something put on — the verb is the one for tying on a servant's apron. The anxiety that follows is not suppressed but handed over 'because he cares for you,' which is C18's freedom from what one is grasping, and the posture of the weaned child in C22's psalm.

entries.pericope: Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful
entries.connection: The two verbs of the desert watchman in one line — be sober, be watchful — with the danger pictured as something circling rather than something already inside. The counsel is steadiness ('withstand him steadfast') and solidarity with others under the same pressure, not anxious self-scrutiny, which is the tone C20 insists on. The promise that follows is restoration after 'a little while,' not exemption.
